package_info.package_versions: All private packages created before October 20th (for leak); All packages (for improper authorization flaw)
package_info.why_malicious: The registry-level flaws enabled attackers to enumerate private package names—exposing sensitive internal project information and enabling targeted dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks—and to publish new versions of any npm package without proper authorization, potentially allowing malicious code injection into legitimate packages and widespread supply chain compromise.

execution_context.trigger: npm registry maintenance event (server-side process updating public change feed)
required_permissions: read access to public npm replica feed (no authentication required)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: During registry maintenance, records containing the names of private npm packages (e.g., '@owner/private-package') were inadvertently published to the public changes feed at replicate.npmjs.com, making them accessible to anyone monitoring the feed.
malicious_snippets.code_language: N/A (data exposure via registry feed, not executable code)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Leaked the names of private npm packages to the public replica feed, exposing confidential package metadata to any external observer and enabling enumeration of internal projects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Private package names are intended to remain confidential within an organization. Their exposure in a public feed allows attackers to discover internal project names, which can be used for targeted dependency confusion, typosquatting, or reconnaissance.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is that private package metadata, including names and scopes, is never published to any public registry endpoint. In this case, private names were exposed in a public, unauthenticated feed.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for exposing private package names in a public feed; such information should always remain internal to the organization.
key_indicators: Presence of scoped private package names (e.g., '@org/private-pkg') in public change feed
Private package metadata visible in replicate.npmjs.com
Unusual increase in enumeration or scraping activity targeting the public changes feed

execution_context.trigger: npm package publish request (API call to registry)
execution_context.file_location: npm registry microservices (authorization and publishing services, specifically the interaction between the authorization endpoint and the publishing endpoint)
required_permissions: ability to upload a package to the npm registry (authenticated account, but not necessarily maintainer of target package)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: A logic flaw in the npm registry allowed an attacker to publish a new version of any package by crafting a publish request where the authorization service validated the user against the package name in the URL, but the publishing service used the package name from the uploaded tarball. This mismatch enabled unauthorized users to publish to packages they did not own.
malicious_snippets.code_language: N/A (logic flaw in registry service interaction, not a code sample)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Allowed attackers to publish new versions of any npm package, including those they did not maintain, by exploiting a mismatch between authorization and publishing logic—potentially injecting malicious code into widely used packages.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Publishing new versions of a package should be strictly limited to authorized maintainers. This flaw allowed any authenticated user to publish to any package, bypassing all ownership and maintainer checks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal registry behavior is to enforce that only listed maintainers can publish new versions of a package. Here, the registry failed to enforce this, allowing unauthorized users to overwrite or add new versions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate scenario where a non-maintainer should be able to publish to a package they do not own. All legitimate publish actions should be performed by authorized maintainers only.
key_indicators: Publish events where the uploader is not listed as a maintainer of the target package
Discrepancy between package name in API URL and package name in uploaded tarball
Unexpected new versions of popular packages published from previously unseen or unrelated accounts

attack_chain.action: Attacker monitors the public npm replica feed (replicate.npmjs.com) to enumerate private package names leaked during registry maintenance.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains knowledge of internal/private package names, enabling targeted attacks.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses the leaked private package names to perform dependency confusion or typosquatting attacks by publishing malicious packages with similar or identical names to the public registry.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victims may install malicious packages, believing them to be legitimate internal dependencies.

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits the authorization flaw in the npm registry to publish new versions of legitimate packages without being an authorized maintainer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is injected into widely used packages, potentially compromising downstream users and the software supply chain.

behavioral_signatures: Enumeration or scraping of private package names from public npm replica feeds
Publish events for packages where the uploader is not listed as a maintainer
Sudden appearance of new versions of popular packages published by previously unseen or unrelated accounts
Unusual spikes in package installs or downloads for packages with names similar to internal/private packages
file_indicators: Private package names (scoped as '@org/package') present in public change feeds (replicate.npmjs.com)
Unexpected package version updates in the registry without corresponding maintainer activity
Discrepancy between package name in publish API URL and package name in uploaded tarball
network_indicators: Automated or high-frequency access to replicate.npmjs.com for the purpose of package name enumeration
Unusual or unauthorized API calls to npm registry endpoints for package publishing, especially from accounts not associated with the target package
Publish requests where the authenticated user does not match the package's maintainer list
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor the public npm replica feed (replicate.npmjs.com) for the presence of private or scoped package names. Audit all publish events to verify that the uploader is an authorized maintainer of the target package, and flag any publish attempts where this is not the case. Correlate publish API requests to ensure the package name in the URL matches the name in the uploaded tarball. Watch for spikes in installs or the creation of new packages with names similar to known internal/private packages, which may indicate dependency confusion or typosquatting attempts.
